analysis.one_liner: Restricts meatpackers' use of opaque, formula-priced forward contracts to buy cattle and hogs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after bipartisan introduction in 2003, the Senate Agriculture Committee took no action, and it died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Large meatpacking companies buy a growing share of cattle and hogs through 'captive supply' — forward contracts where the price is set later by a formula, so ranchers can't see what their animals are really worth before they sell. This bill would have banned formula-priced forward contracts, required every contract to carry a firm base price in actual dollars, forced packers to offer contracts through open public bidding where more than one buyer can bid, and capped most forward contracts at 40 cattle or 30 hogs. It was introduced in May 2003 and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent livestock producers — ranchers and hog farmers who sell to meatpackers. The bill would have forced packers to bid openly for contracted animals with a fixed base price, giving producers a real market price instead of a formula they can't verify, and limiting the volume of livestock packers can lock up through contracts [S3]. Fewer captive supply arrangements could also strengthen price discovery in cash markets, which sets the benchmark price for all livestock sales.

how_it_helps.text: Every forward contract would have to include a firm base price that equals a fixed dollar amount on the day the contract is signed, so a seller knows what the deal is worth up front [S3].

Contracts would have to be offered through open, public bidding with at least two bids solicited and bids that buyers and sellers can witness, instead of the private, negotiated deals that currently dominate [S3].

Formula-based pricing — where the price is calculated later from information the seller can't see — would be prohibited, though pricing based on futures markets or verifiable quality factors outside the packer's control would remain allowed [S3].
Forward contracts would be capped at 40 cattle or 30 hogs per contract, limiting how much livestock a packer can lock up in advance through a single deal [S3].
The CRS summary confirms the bill would amend the Packers and Stockyards Act to require fixed base pricing and public bidding, prohibit formula pricing, and limit contract size [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies, which would lose the ability to buy livestock through private formula-priced contracts. Their contracting costs would rise and their flexibility to secure steady supplies at negotiated prices would shrink. Larger producers who benefit from the current contracting system, or who use formula contracts with favored packers, would also face restrictions.

drawbacks.text: The limits apply to contracts covering more than 40 cattle or 30 hogs, so larger feeding and finishing operations that rely on forward contracts to manage risk and guarantee sales would lose a tool they currently use, not just packers [S3].

Banning formula pricing outright while carving out futures-market pricing and verifiable quality adjustments creates a line that is partly arbitrary: contracts based on futures prices can still obscure a deal's final value, so some of the price-discovery problem the bill targets would remain [S3].

Restricting captive supply contracting could add costs for packers and complicate supply planning for large-scale production, costs that could be passed back through the supply chain rather than absorbed by the packers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core benefit — forcing open, fixed-price bidding on livestock contracts so producers can see real prices — addresses a long-standing complaint of independent ranchers about packer-dominated markets. Its main weakness is design: the carve-out for futures-based pricing and the relatively low contract caps draw lines that don't perfectly separate fair contracting from captive supply, and larger producers would lose flexibility alongside the packers. On balance it is a targeted competition measure aimed at a concentrated buyer side of the market, not a broad restriction on livestock trade.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2003 and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never held a vote on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Enzi introduced the Captive Supply Reform Act in the Senate on May 13, 2003, joined by five cosponsors [S5].
The bill had bipartisan sponsorship: Enzi and Sen. Thomas were Republicans, while Dorgan, Johnson, Daschle, and Conrad were Democrats — five cosponsors in all, four Democrats and one Republican [S4].
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never reported the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor for a vote before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking companies come out ahead: they kept their ability to buy livestock through private formula-priced forward contracts, with no bidding requirements or volume limits, because the bill never moved out of committee.

for.name: Sen. Michael B. Enzi
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and took no recorded action on it for the remainder of the Congress — no markup, no report, no vote

against.name: Meatpacking industry
against.what_they_did: Long opposed captive supply restrictions that would limit packers' use of formula-priced forward contracts and captive supplies

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — one Republican sponsor, four Democratic and one Republican cosponsors — but no committee or floor votes were ever recorded, so the partisan shape of the opposition never showed up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have banned packers' formula-priced forward contracts, required open public bidding, and capped contract sizes, directly restricting the tool packers use to secure captive supplies at negotiated prices. Packers' gain under the status quo — buying through private contracts rather than open bids — is the price-discovery loss producers complain about.

The bill deliberately excluded futures-based pricing from its definition of 'formula price,' so contracts pegged to futures markets would remain legal. This steers price-setting toward a transparent public market rather than private formulas.

Operations selling more than 40 cattle or 30 hogs under forward contracts would have faced the same bidding and pricing rules, limiting their contracting flexibility. Some large producers would bear compliance burdens alongside packers.
